seeds.asked: Describe the sympathetic supply of abdominal and pelvic viscera. (8 marks)
seeds.label: The sympathetic outflow to the gut and pelvis leaves the cord as splanchnic nerves and relays in the collateral ganglia before riding the blood vessels to the organ
seeds.definition: Sympathetic supply to the abdominal viscera arises as preganglionic fibres from T5-T12, passing through the paravertebral chain without relay and leaving as splanchnic nerves (greater, T5-T9, to coeliac and superior mesenteric ganglia; lesser, T10-T11, to aorticorenal and superior mesenteric ganglia; least, T12, to the aorticorenal ganglion); postganglionic fibres then run with the blood vessels to the abdominal viscera, relaxing gut plain muscle and contracting sphincters, constricting most abdominal arterioles, driving hepatic glycogenolysis, contracting the splenic capsule to release stored blood, and stimulating the adrenal medulla. Sympathetic supply to the pelvic viscera arises as preganglionic fibres from T12-L2, reaching the inferior mesenteric ganglion as lumbar splanchnic nerves for the gut and the sacral ganglia as sacral splanchnic nerves for the bladder and genitalia; postganglionic fibres relax the distal colon and rectum while contracting the internal anal sphincter (retaining faeces), relax the bladder wall while contracting the internal urethral sphincter (retaining urine), and contract the vas deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate to produce ejaculation.
seeds.objective: State the segmental origin, relay ganglia and course of the sympathetic supply to the abdominal and to the pelvic viscera, and give the main functional effect on each organ named.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming abdominal and pelvic sympathetic fibres relay the same way. Abdominal preganglionic fibres pass the paravertebral chain untouched and relay in collateral ganglia named after the great vessels; pelvic fibres to the gut do the same via the inferior mesenteric ganglion, but the fibres to bladder and genitalia instead leave via the sacral ganglia as sacral splanchnic nerves.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Sympathetic nervous system

seeds.asked: Describe the parasympathetic supply of head and neck. (6 marks)
seeds.label: Three cranial nerves — III, VII and IX — carry the parasympathetic supply to the head and neck, each with its own brainstem nucleus, relay ganglion and target gland or muscle
seeds.definition: The oculomotor nerve (III) carries preganglionic fibres from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain, relaying in the ciliary ganglion; postganglionic fibres run as short ciliary nerves to contract the constrictor pupillae (miosis) and the ciliary muscle (accommodation for near vision). The facial nerve (VII) carries preganglionic fibres from the superior salivary nucleus in the lower pons; some relay in the sphenopalatine ganglion, whose postganglionic fibres supply the lacrimal and nasal glands, and others run in the chorda tympani to relay in the submandibular ganglion, whose postganglionic fibres supply the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands — functions secretomotor and vasodilator. The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carries preganglionic fibres from the inferior salivary nucleus at the pons-medulla junction, relaying in the otic ganglion, whose postganglionic fibres supply the parotid gland — again secretomotor and vasodilator.
seeds.objective: Name the three cranial nerves that carry the parasympathetic supply to the head and neck, and for each give the brainstem nucleus of origin, the relay ganglion, and what it supplies.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming the facial nerve relays in only one ganglion. It splits: fibres via the sphenopalatine ganglion serve the lacrimal and nasal glands, while fibres via the chorda tympani relay separately in the submandibular ganglion for the submandibular and sublingual glands.
seeds.subject: neuro
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Autonomic nervous system > Parasympathetic nervous system

seeds.asked: Explain the mechanism of iron absorption. Mention the effect of iron deficiency and its causes. (10 marks)
seeds.label: Iron crosses the enterocyte by two doors, DMT1 for the ferrous ion and HCP1 for haem, and whether it goes to storage or to the blood depends on the body's need; too little iron, from any of three causes, gives a small pale RBC
seeds.definition: Iron is absorbed by enterocytes, mainly in the duodenum. At the apical membrane, ferrous iron (Fe2+) enters via divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1) — ferric iron not reduced in the stomach is reduced to Fe2+ in the duodenum by a reductase — while haem iron enters via a separate carrier, haem carrier protein 1 (HCP1). Inside the enterocyte, if body demand is decreased, most iron is stored as ferritin and haemosiderin and lost with the sloughed enterocyte in the faeces; if demand is increased, iron crosses the basolateral membrane via the export protein ferroportin, is oxidised to Fe3+ by a ferroxidase, and binds plasma transferrin (normally 35% saturated), which delivers it to transferrin-receptor-bearing cells of marrow, liver and muscle. Iron deficiency produces microcytic hypochromic anaemia — decreased RBC mass and haemoglobin content, MCV under 80 fL and MCH under 25 pg — from three causes: dietary deficiency (low intake, more common in growing children and pregnancy), deficient absorption (partial gastrectomy, vitamin C deficiency, excess phytate/oxalate/phosphate, small-intestinal disease), and chronic blood loss (hookworm infestation, bleeding peptic ulcer or piles, excessive menstrual bleeding).
seeds.objective: Trace iron from the gut lumen to plasma transferrin through both possible enterocyte fates, then name the three causes of iron deficiency and the anaemia it produces.
seeds.pitfall: Treating DMT1 as the only iron door into the enterocyte. Haem iron uses a separate transporter, HCP1, so a diet's absorbable iron is the sum of both routes, and this is why haem iron (meat) is absorbed more efficiently than the non-haem iron that depends on reduction and DMT1 alone.
seeds.subject: haem

seeds.asked: Case: (6 marks; each question 1 mark). A 31-year-old patient presented to emergency room with dyspnea and acute chest pain. He was diagnosed as acute pulmonary embolism secondary to deep venous thrombosis. The physician prescribed to him tissue plasminogen activator. Further investigation proved that this patient has activated protein C resistance. Questions: a) Outline the mechanism of action of tissue plasminogen activator. b) Inside the body, explain the relation between protein C and tissue plasminogen activator. c) Clarify the role of thrombin in coagulation. d) How does thrombin lose its procoagulant activity and become a potent anticoagulant? e) Name the factors inactivated by protein C. f) Name 2 possible complications of blood clot formation inside blood vessels.
seeds.label: The fibrinolytic system turns the same enzyme, thrombin, from the maker of the clot into the trigger of its own dissolution once it is bound to endothelial thrombomodulin
seeds.definition: Thrombin has two opposite roles. Procoagulant: thrombin, formed from prothrombin by the prothrombin activator complex of active factor X, phospholipid, calcium and active factor V, converts fibrinogen to fibrin and drives the coagulation cascade. Anticoagulant: when thrombin binds thrombomodulin, expressed by endothelial cells (except cerebral microcirculation), the thrombin-thrombomodulin complex activates protein C; activated protein C (APC), with cofactor protein S, inactivates factors V and VIIIa and inactivates the inhibitor of tissue plasminogen activator (TPA), so that activated TPA converts plasminogen to plasmin (with thrombin's help), and plasmin lyses fibrin and fibrinogen into fibrinogen degradation products, which themselves inhibit thrombin. Activated protein C resistance means factor V is not properly inactivated by APC, so this fibrinolytic brake fails and the patient over-clots, producing this case's deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
seeds.objective: Trace thrombin's dual role in coagulation and in its own fibrinolytic shutdown via protein C, and explain why a defect in protein C's action on factor V causes a clotting tendency.
seeds.pitfall: Treating protein C and TPA as unrelated. Activated protein C's job is precisely to unblock TPA by inactivating TPA's own inhibitor, so protein C resistance leaves both factor Va active and TPA suppressed — a double push toward clot.
seeds.subject: haem
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Physiology > Blood > Physiological limitations of blood coagulation

seeds.asked: Point mutation may have no effect or may cause serious effects. (6 marks)
seeds.label: A base substitution is missense, nonsense or silent, and only the label tells you whether the protein is unchanged, wrecked or truncated
seeds.definition: Base substitutions are the commonest gene mutations. A nonsense mutation converts an amino acid codon into a stop codon, so translation terminates prematurely and the protein product is usually non-functional — thalassaemia is the example. A missense mutation changes the codon so a different amino acid is inserted; the effect ranges from none to very serious, as in sickle cell anaemia, where glutamate is replaced by valine at position six of the beta chain. A silent mutation gives a synonym codon for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged.
seeds.objective: Name the three types of point mutation and explain why the same class of change (a single base substitution) can range from harmless to fatal.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming every missense mutation is harmless because only one amino acid changes. Whether it matters depends on which amino acid — swapping polar glutamate for nonpolar valine is exactly what produces sickle cell anaemia.
seeds.subject: fnd

seeds.asked: cAMP acts as a hormone second messenger. (6 marks)
seeds.label: A hormone that cannot enter the cell hands its message to adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP, which switches protein kinase A on, and that one relay explains how glucagon and epinephrine push glycogen breakdown while insulin pushes it back
seeds.definition: cAMP is formed from ATP by adenylyl cyclase and broken down to AMP by phosphodiesterase. Hormone-receptor interaction activates G proteins, which activate adenylyl cyclase, generating cAMP. Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase A: the inactive enzyme is a tetramer of two regulatory and two catalytic subunits, and binding of two cAMP molecules to each regulatory subunit releases the active catalytic subunits, which phosphorylate substrate enzymes, activating some and inactivating others; a protein phosphatase reverses this by dephosphorylation. Glucagon and epinephrine act through this mechanism, raising cAMP, while insulin lowers cAMP by activating protein phosphatase and phosphodiesterase.
seeds.objective: Trace the chain from hormone-receptor binding to phosphorylated-enzyme effect, and explain how insulin reverses what glucagon and epinephrine do through this same pathway.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming cAMP itself does the phosphorylating. cAMP's job is to release the catalytic subunits of protein kinase A from its regulatory subunits — the kinase does the phosphorylation.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Free Nucleotides

seeds.asked: Collagen molecule has a strong flexible structure. (6 marks)
seeds.label: Collagen is strong because every level of its structure is built for tightness — three residues per turn, glycine in every third position, a right-handed superhelix of left-handed chains, hydroxyproline hydrogen bonds, and covalent cross-links between chains
seeds.definition: Tropocollagen is three left-handed alpha-chains twisted into a right-handed superhelix, each chain the repeating triplet Gly-X-Y. Strength comes from: only 3 residues per turn (tighter than an ordinary protein's 3.6); glycine at every third position, small enough to let the chains pack close; the high hydroxyproline content forming interchain hydrogen bonds; covalent cross-links between adjacent chains giving tensile strength; and the staggered fibril/fibre arrangement giving flexibility.
seeds.objective: List the structural features, from the amino-acid triplet up to the fibre, that together give collagen its tensile strength and flexibility.
seeds.pitfall: Crediting proline alone for the strength. Proline prevents a right-handed helix in the single chain, but glycine's small size is what lets three chains pack close enough to superhelix together.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Proteins of Extracellular Matrix

seeds.asked: Trimming is a very important posttranslational modification. (Explain and mention an example.) (6 marks)
seeds.label: Trimming cuts an inactive precursor protein down to its active, functional size, and insulin and the zymogens are two worked examples
seeds.definition: Many proteins are synthesised as larger, inactive precursor molecules; portions of the chain must then be removed by specific endoproteases to release the active protein — this is trimming. Examples: preproinsulin is converted to proinsulin and then to insulin; and zymogens, the inactive precursors of secreted enzymes, are activated by trimming — trypsinogen is activated to trypsin in the small intestine.
seeds.objective: Explain why trimming is needed (an inactive precursor becomes active) and give one worked example.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming trimming is the same thing as the covalent side-chain modifications (phosphorylation, glycosylation, hydroxylation, carboxylation). Trimming is proteolytic — it removes a piece of the polypeptide backbone itself, rather than adding or altering a side group.
seeds.subject: fnd

seeds.label: DNA and RNA differ across every dimension — bases, sugar, strandedness, kind, location and job
seeds.definition: Comparing the two across every dimension: bases — both have adenine, guanine, cytosine; DNA has thymine and no uracil, RNA has uracil and thymine only as a minor tRNA base. Sugar — DNA 2-deoxyribose, RNA ribose. Shape — DNA double helix, RNA single strand. Types — DNA linear/circular, RNA is mRNA/tRNA/rRNA. Site — DNA nucleus and mitochondria, RNA mainly cytosol. Function — DNA carries genetic information and directs RNA synthesis, RNA carries out protein synthesis.
seeds.objective: Reproduce the DNA-versus-RNA comparison across bases, sugar, strand shape, types, site and function.
seeds.pitfall: Saying RNA never contains thymine. Thymine appears in RNA too, as a minor base specifically in tRNA.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Chemistry of Nucleic Acids

seeds.label: not established — this topic is not covered in the assigned source for this module
seeds.definition: The assigned source for this module does not mention lactate dehydrogenase, creatine kinase, isoenzymes, or cardiac/muscle enzyme markers anywhere in it. No source-backed definition can be written for this question.
seeds.objective: Not established from the assigned source.

seeds.subject: fnd

seeds.label: Myoglobin is a one-heme oxygen store built for muscle, hemoglobin is a four-heme oxygen taxi built for blood, and their oxygen-affinity curves are shaped by exactly that difference in job
seeds.definition: Site: myoglobin in cardiac and skeletal muscle; hemoglobin (HbA1) in red blood cells. Structure: myoglobin one heme + one chain (153 aa, 8 helices); hemoglobin four heme rings + four chains (alpha 141 aa/7 helices, beta 146 aa/8 helices). Function: myoglobin stores O2 and releases it during severe exercise; hemoglobin transports O2 to tissue, removes CO2, buffers blood. Affinity: myoglobin higher at low pO2; hemoglobin higher at the lung, lower at the tissue. Clinical: myoglobin a marker of muscle damage; HbA1c assesses 3-month diabetic control.
seeds.objective: Compare myoglobin and hemoglobin by site, structure, function and oxygen affinity, and explain why the affinity difference suits each protein's job.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming higher oxygen affinity makes myoglobin the better carrier. Its high, flat affinity curve is exactly why it is a poor transporter and a good store.
seeds.subject: haem

seeds.label: Lysine, arginine and histidine are the basic (diamino-monocarboxylic) amino acids
seeds.definition: The basic (diamino-monocarboxylic) amino acids are lysine, arginine and histidine.
seeds.pitfall: Confusing 'basic' (charge) with 'essential' (diet). Basic here means the R group is positively charged (an extra amino group); lysine, arginine and histidine happen to also be nutritionally essential/semi-essential, but the classification asked for is chemical.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Amino Acids of Biological Importance

seeds.label: Linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are the two fatty acids the body cannot make and must eat
seeds.definition: Essential fatty acids cannot be synthesised in the body and must come from the diet: alpha-linolenic acid and linoleic acid. Arachidonic acid is normally made from linoleic acid, becoming essential itself only if linoleic acid is deficient.
seeds.objective: Name the two essential fatty acids and explain why arachidonic acid is only conditionally essential.
seeds.pitfall: Naming arachidonic acid as essential outright. It is normally synthesised from linoleic acid and becomes essential only when linoleic acid is deficient.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Lipids of Biological Importance

seeds.asked: Two causes of gene mutations. (2 marks)
seeds.label: A mutation starts either as a replication mistake or as chemical/radiation/oxidative damage to the DNA itself
seeds.definition: Causes of mutations: (1) errors in replication — a non-complementary base added and not repaired; (2) damage to DNA nucleotides, which includes chemical mutagens (e.g. cigarette-smoke carcinogens), irradiation (UV, X-rays, gamma rays) and oxidative damage (implicated in neurological disease, cancer and ageing).
seeds.objective: Name two causes of gene mutation.
seeds.pitfall: Treating 'damage of nucleotides' as one single cause. It splits into three: chemical mutagens, irradiation and oxidative damage, alongside the separate cause of uncorrected replication error.
seeds.subject: fnd

seeds.label: Starch and glycogen are two homopolysaccharides, both built entirely of glucose
seeds.definition: Homopolysaccharides are built entirely of one monosaccharide type; the glucans (glucose) are starch, glycogen and cellulose, and the fructans (fructose) include inulin.
seeds.objective: Name two homopolysaccharides and their monosaccharide unit.
seeds.pitfall: Naming a heteropolysaccharide (e.g. a GAG such as heparin) as a homopolysaccharide.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Carbohydrates of Biological Importance

seeds.label: Sickle cell anemia and thalassemia are two named hemoglobinopathies, one from a wrong amino acid and one from too little chain
seeds.definition: Hemoglobinopathies are caused either by structurally abnormal globin chains, e.g. sickle cell anemia (HbS), or by an abnormally reduced amount of alpha or beta globin chains, e.g. the thalassaemias.
seeds.pitfall: Treating sickle cell anemia and thalassemia as the same mechanism; one is a structural defect, the other a quantity defect.
seeds.subject: haem

seeds.asked: Two factors affecting the rate of enzyme catalyzed reaction. (2 marks)
seeds.label: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction is set by substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, cofactor concentration, temperature and pH
seeds.definition: Five factors govern enzyme reaction velocity: substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, cofactor concentration, temperature (optimum near 37C) and pH (usually 5-9).
seeds.objective: Name two of the five factors affecting enzyme reaction rate.
seeds.pitfall: Assuming higher temperature always means faster reaction; past the optimum the enzyme denatures and velocity falls.
seeds.subject: fnd

seeds.asked: Four effects of denaturation on proteins. (4 marks)
seeds.label: Denaturation ruptures the bonds holding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure, leaving the primary sequence intact but the protein insoluble, more viscous, more digestible and biologically dead
seeds.definition: Denaturation breaks the bonds stabilising secondary/tertiary/quaternary structure, leaving only the primary structure. Effects: decreased solubility, increased viscosity, increased digestibility by proteolytic enzymes, loss of higher-order structure, loss of biological activity, loss of antigenic property.
seeds.objective: List four effects of denaturation on a protein.
seeds.pitfall: Saying the peptide bonds are broken; the primary structure survives denaturation, which is why the protein becomes more, not less, digestible.
seeds.subject: fnd
seeds.modulePath: 102 INT > Biochemistry > Proteins of Biological Importance
